passage:
Faculty mentor's note, second-year engineering, 9 October. Sunaina.
Anirban came to my office hour today, not about his project. He said he has been sleeping badly for about five weeks, missed two lab submissions, and stopped calling home because "there's nothing good to report." Then he asked, "Is this serious enough to see someone, or am I overreacting?" I told him that trouble which lasts for weeks and spills into sleep, studies and the people he loves is exactly the time to see a professional. I also asked whether he'd had any thoughts of harming himself. He said no, and I told him that if that ever changes, it's a reason to get help the same day.
What I did next: we opened the campus wellness portal together, and he booked a counsellor for Monday. I've also emailed him the health centre doctor's hours.

qa.a: About five weeks.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel when he came to the office hour?
qa.a: He felt unsure and a bit embarrassed, wondering whether it was serious enough or whether he was overreacting.

qa.q: What first step did Sunaina help Anirban take?
qa.a: They opened the campus wellness portal together and Anirban booked a counsellor for Monday.

qa.q: What might it mean for the people at home that Anirban stopped calling?
qa.a: They may be missing him and wondering why, which shows the struggle is already touching his relationships.

grounding: It shows a mentor recognising that weeks of struggle affecting sleep, studies and family calls mean it is time for professional help, and using campus services for the first step.

passage:
Sunday, late
Made a list tonight because my head won't hold thoughts in order.
- About a month of waking up already exhausted.
- Missed three shifts at the bakery. Told my manager I had a fever. I didn't.
- Haven't opened my statistics notes in two weeks.
- Snapped at Nandini over the dishes, and she's the kindest roommate alive.
I kept telling myself it's just a rough patch. But written down, it's been weeks and it's touching everything.
Nandini knocked while I was writing. I showed her the list instead of saying "I'm fine." She didn't panic. She said her cousin went through something like this and the student health centre helped. We booked the doctor for ten tomorrow morning on the college portal. She's coming with me.
First step. I feel lighter already, or maybe just less alone.
Indu

qa.a: Three shifts at the bakery.

qa.a: Relieved and lighter, or at least less alone.

qa.a: Indu showed Nandini the list instead of saying "I'm fine", and together they booked the student health doctor.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt being snapped at over the dishes?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt or puzzled, but seeing the list helped her understand it was part of a bigger struggle.

grounding: It shows a young adult noticing that weeks of low mood are affecting sleep, work, study and a roommate, and taking the first step to a doctor with support.

passage: Jagdish, twenty, helped on the family farm by day and studied for his correspondence degree at night. For six weeks now, he hadn't slept properly. He had stopped opening his books, shouted at his mother over nothing and skipped the village cricket match he loved. Trisha, the teacher at the village school who had tutored him years ago, noticed him sitting alone by the pump. "Jagdish, you've looked lost for weeks. Your sleep, your studies, your temper, all changed." He shrugged. "Just tired." "When it goes on this long and touches everything, that's the time to see someone. The doctor at the health centre can help, and they can refer you to a counsellor." The next morning she went with him on the bus.

qa.q: How long had Jagdish not slept properly?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: How had Jagdish been feeling lately?
qa.a: He had been low, irritable and worn out, shouting at his mother and losing interest in cricket.

qa.q: What did Trisha do that helped Jagdish take the first step?
qa.a: She named the signs, explained that a long struggle affecting everything means it's time for help, and went with him to the health centre doctor.

qa.q: How might Jagdish's mother have felt when he shouted at her?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt and confused, not knowing he was struggling.

grounding: Shows a trusted adult recognising weeks of struggle affecting sleep, study and relationships as a sign to seek help, and helping with the first step.

passage: In Copenhagen, Lars, twenty-one, had been struggling since autumn. He slept badly, missed seminars and had cancelled dinner with Noa three times. "It's just the dark months," he told her. Noa wasn't convinced. Over coffee she said, "It's been weeks. You're not sleeping, you're not studying, and you're avoiding everyone. When it touches all of that, it's time to talk to a professional. Not because you're weak." Lars stirred his coffee. "I wouldn't even know where to start." "The student health service. They have counsellors and a doctor. I'll look up the number now." She did, and he called from the café, voice unsteady. The appointment was for Thursday. He let out a long breath.

qa.q: How many times had Lars cancelled dinner with Noa?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: How did Lars feel when he called from the café?
qa.a: He felt nervous and unsure, his voice unsteady, then relieved once the appointment was booked.

qa.q: What made Noa's approach effective?
qa.a: She named the lasting signs affecting sleep, study and relationships, explained that meant seeing a professional and helped him find the student health service.

qa.q: How might Noa have felt when Lars kept blaming the dark months?
qa.a: Noa likely felt worried and unconvinced, which is why she spoke up.

grounding: Shows a friend recognising weeks of struggle affecting sleep, study and relationships as the time to see a professional, and helping find campus services.

passage:
At the campus wellness centre in Kolkata, Ujjwal filled in the form with a shaky pen. Reason for visit: I don't know if this counts.
Leela, the counsellor, read it and smiled. "Tell me what's been happening."
"For about six weeks I've barely slept. I've missed three labs. I snapped at my roommate over nothing. I keep thinking I should just push through."
"Six weeks, sleep, study and your relationships. That counts," Leela said. "When struggles last that long and spill into your life like that, it's exactly the time to come in."
Ujjwal let out a long breath. "I nearly didn't."
"I'm glad you did. We'll meet weekly, and I'll connect you with the campus doctor about the sleep. And if you ever have thoughts of hurting yourself, come here or call the helpline straight away, any time."
Ujjwal nodded, and for the first time in weeks he felt a little lighter.

qa.q: How many labs had Ujjwal missed?
qa.a: Three labs.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when Leela said his situation counts?
qa.a: He felt relieved, letting out a long breath, and a little lighter for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: What signs showed it was time for Ujjwal to seek help?
qa.a: His struggles had lasted about six weeks and were affecting his sleep, studies and relationships.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal's roommate see the change once he gets support?
qa.a: The roommate may feel relieved to see him less snappy and understand the outbursts came from stress, not dislike.

grounding: Ujjwal's weeks of poor sleep, missed labs and strained relationships are signs it is time, and a campus counsellor helps him take the first step.
